summary: Arabic is a Semitic language. This course teaches Modern Standard Arabic, the shared written and formal language of the Arab world; everyday speech is in regional dialects. It is written from right to left, and words are built from consonant roots.

typology.why: Words are built by weaving a consonant root into a vowel pattern (k-t-b: كَتَبَ kataba ‘he wrote’, كِتَاب kitāb ‘book’), and one ending carries person, number and gender at once.
typology.alsoShows: Small words are attached in front or behind like pieces: وَ wa- ‘and’, الْ al- ‘the’, possessive endings.

facts.label: Script
facts.value: Arabic script, right to left; letters join and change shape; short vowels are usually not written

facts.label: Where
facts.value: official language of more than 20 countries from Morocco to Iraq; the language of the Qur’an

peculiarities.title: Roots and patterns
peculiarities.text: Most words share a root of three consonants with their relatives; the vowels and extra letters around it give the meaning.

peculiarities.title: No ‘to be’ in the present
peculiarities.text: أَنَا طَالِبٌ ʾana ṭālibun = ‘I (am) a student’: the present tense of ‘to be’ is not said.

peculiarities.title: Unwritten vowels
peculiarities.text: Short vowels are marks above and below the letters; normal texts leave them out. This course shows them until you can read without them.

peculiarities.title: Gender everywhere
peculiarities.text: Two genders, and ‘you’, verbs and adjectives change with them: أَنْتَ anta (to a man), أَنْتِ anti (to a woman).

quiz.why: Roots woven into patterns, and endings that carry several meanings at once.

quiz.q: How do you say ‘I am a student’?
options: with the verb كَانَ in the present
quiz.why: The present of ‘to be’ is not said.

quiz.q: What do كِتَاب, كَاتِب and كَتَبَ have in common?
quiz.why: All three are built on the root of ‘writing’.

notes.text: Familiar: grammatical gender, agreement, case endings (Arabic has three: -u, -a, -i, roughly your nominative, accusative and genitive) and an article for things in general: أُحِبُّ الْقَهْوَةَ = μου αρέσει ο καφές. Arabic ث and ذ are your θ and δ, and the old letter order أ ب ج د matches α β γ δ; قَلَم (pen) goes back to κάλαμος. New: no neuter, no word for “a”, no capital letters, only three vowel qualities (a, i, u — short and long), sounds such as ع، ح، ق, and one past form for έφαγα and έχω φάει.

Easy: one definite article (الْ) and many shared words — algebra, alcohol, sugar, coffee, cotton came into English from or through Arabic. Hard: a new script with no capital letters, two genders that also mark “you”, person endings on every verb, three cases, the dual, and short vowels that are not written. Arabic does not reduce unstressed vowels (كِتَابٌ is ki-tā-bun), has no phrasal verbs (خَرَجَ = go out), and one past form covers “I ate” and “I have eaten”.

You already learn nouns with their gender and plural and verbs with person endings — the same habits work here. Like German, Arabic needs no article with a job: Ich bin Lehrer = أَنَا مُعَلِّمٌ. The ach-Laut is Arabic خ, and the glottal stop before a vowel (be-achten) is the hamza ء. Different: no “is” in the present, two genders, no capital letters, no ü or ö (three vowel qualities only), no final devoicing (the d of وَلَد stays d), no separable prefixes, one past form for ich aß and ich habe gegessen, and no verb-second rule: the verb may come first (VSO) and never moves in a subordinate clause.

Russian has no present “to be” either: Я студент = أَنَا طَالِبٌ, word for word; the past shows the gender, as был / была = كَانَ / كَانَتْ; and “I have” is “at me (is)”: у меня есть ≈ عِنْدِي. Russian х is Arabic خ. Different: Arabic has a definite article (الْ), three cases instead of six, no capital letters, no hard / soft consonant pairs, no vowel reduction (every vowel keeps its sound), no final devoicing and no aspect prefixes on verbs.

Thousands of Turkish words are Arabic — kitap (كِتَاب), kalem (قَلَم), merhaba (مَرْحَبًا), selam (سَلَام), sabah (صَبَاح), insan (إِنْسَان), muallim (مُعَلِّم), saat (سَاعَة): your best bridge, and Ottoman Turkish was written in this script until 1928. Like Turkish, Arabic puts possessive endings on nouns (كِتَابِي ≈ kitabım) and needs no separate “to be” in the present. Hard: gender everywhere, even on “you”; changes inside the word instead of a chain of suffixes; no vowel harmony (endings keep their vowels) and no ü or ö; no final devoicing (kitap, but كِتَاب with b); no capital letters; few compounds like yardım etmek — “to help” is one verb, سَاعَدَ; no evidential or surprise -miş; and no -ip / -ince converbs — clauses are joined with words like وَ and عِنْدَمَا.

Hundreds of Spanish words come from Arabic, many with the article al- fused in: aceite (الزَّيْت), azúcar (السُّكَّر), arroz (الْأَرُزّ), alcachofa (الْخُرْشُوف), berenjena (بَاذِنْجَان), and ojalá (لَوْ شَاءَ اللّٰهُ). Familiar: two genders, agreement, adjectives after the noun (casa grande = بَيْتٌ كَبِيرٌ). New: three cases, the dual, “you” by gender, no capital letters, no verb “to be” in the present (so no ser / estar choice), three vowel qualities instead of five, and one past form for comí and he comido.

Familiar: two genders and no neuter, the article for things in general (j’aime le café = أُحِبُّ الْقَهْوَةَ), adjectives mostly after the noun, and chez, which is Arabic عِنْدَ (chez le médecin = عِنْدَ الطَّبِيبِ). French took words from Arabic too: sucre, café, coton, épinard, aubergine, artichaut. New: three cases, the dual, “you” by gender, no “to be” in the present, no capital letters, and no nasal vowels or ü / eu — Arabic has three vowel qualities, short and long.

Hindi took many Arabic words through Persian: किताब kitāb (كِتَاب — feminine in Hindi, masculine in Arabic), दुनिया (دُنْيَا), हाल (حَال, as in كَيْفَ حَالُكَ), लेकिन (لٰكِنْ). Familiar: two genders, “I have” as “near me is” (मेरे पास … है ≈ عِنْدِي) and a question word at the start (क्या ≈ هَلْ). New: prepositions instead of postpositions, three cases on the noun itself, the verb first, and a script read right to left. Arabic has no retroflex or aspirated consonants and no nasal vowels — its ṭ ḍ ṣ ẓ are emphatic (said with the back of the tongue raised), not retroflex —, and few करना-type compounds: “to work” is one verb, عَمِلَ.

Persian is written in the same script (Persian adds پ چ ژ گ) and is full of Arabic words — کتاب, وقت, حال, صبح — so reading will come fast. But Persian says several Arabic letters alike (ث س ص all s; ذ ز ض ظ all z; ح ه both h; ع like a glottal stop), and Arabic keeps them all apart. New: two genders, three cases, the dual, the article الْ, verbs that show the subject’s gender, and few compounds with کردن: Arabic uses single verbs (عَمِلَ, “to work”).

Marathi is written left to right in an abugida; Arabic is an abjad written right to left, with short vowels mostly unwritten. Familiar: grammatical gender (two, not three — no neuter), agreeing adjectives, and possession as “at me” (माझ्याकडे … आहे ≈ عِنْدِي). New: prepositions before the noun instead of postpositions, the verb first, no retroflex and no aspirated consonants, and only one “we”: نَحْنُ covers both आम्ही and आपण.

Hebrew is the closest relative: the same roots (כ־ת־ב / ك ت ب), the same two genders, the article as a prefix (הַ / الْ), no word for “a”, no “to be” in the present, and “I have” with a preposition and a pronoun (יֵשׁ לִי ≈ لِي, عِنْدِي). New in Arabic: three cases, the dual for every noun, broken plurals, plurals of things agreeing as feminine singular, and the sounds ع ح ق ط ص ض ظ, which keep their old, distinct values.

Almost everything is new: letters joined right to left instead of kana and kanji, prepositions before the noun instead of particles after it, the verb first, gender on nouns, verbs and “you”, and plurals that must be marked. Familiar: long and short vowels and double consonants change the meaning (كَتَبَ / كَتَّبَ), as in Japanese. Arabic has three vowel qualities (a, i, u), no pitch accent, no counters (ثَلَاثَةُ كُتُبٍ, three books), few する-type verbs (“to study” is one verb, دَرَسَ), no -te forms, no hearsay forms like 〜そうだ, and no honorific verbs or speech levels: politeness lies in words such as مِنْ فَضْلِكَ and in titles.

New: an alphabet joined right to left, gender, the verb first, prepositions instead of particles, and plurals that must be marked. Familiar: like 아니다, Arabic has a separate word for “is not” (لَيْسَ). Arabic has no aspirated series (ㅋ ㅌ ㅍ), no counters (세 권 → ثَلَاثَةُ كُتُبٍ), few 하다-type verbs (“to study” is one verb, دَرَسَ), no -고 / -서 clause chains, no endings for hearsay or surprise (-대, -네), and no honorific verbs or speech levels: politeness comes from words and titles.

Familiar: possessive endings (kirjani ≈ كِتَابِي), “I have” as “at me” (minulla on ≈ عِنْدِي), and long vowels and double consonants that change the meaning. New: gender, even on “you”; prepositions instead of case endings; changes inside the word, but no consonant gradation; no vowel harmony (endings keep their vowels); no ä, ö, y — three vowel qualities only —; and no capital letters.

Familiar: a definite article before the noun even after “this” — ez a ház = هٰذَا الْبَيْتُ, “this the house” —, possessive endings (házam ≈ بَيْتِي), an object that is always marked (házat ≈ الْبَيْتَ), and long vowels. New: gender, prepositions instead of case endings, the verb first, no vowel harmony, no ü / ö, no preverbs like meg- or el-, and no capital letters.

Swahili took many words from Arabic: kitabu (كِتَاب), saa (سَاعَة), wakati (وَقْت), mwalimu (مُعَلِّم), habari (خَبَر), lakini (لٰكِنْ), and the day names Alhamisi (الْخَمِيس) and Ijumaa (الْجُمُعَة); it was long written in Arabic script. Familiar: the adjective after the noun (kitabu kikubwa ≈ كِتَابٌ كَبِيرٌ), agreement everywhere, and a question word at the start (Je …? ≈ هَلْ). New: two sex-based genders instead of noun classes, endings and inner changes instead of prefixes, no applicative verbs (-ia, -ea), no capital letters, and three vowel qualities instead of five.

Familiar: agreement that runs through the sentence, and long vowels and double consonants that change the meaning (Luganda writes them double; Arabic marks a double consonant with ـّ). New: two sex-based genders instead of noun classes — هُوَ he and هِيَ she where Luganda has ye for both —, changes inside the word and endings instead of prefixes, no applicative verbs, no capital letters, and no tones: pitch never changes the meaning of a word.

Almost everything is new: letters for sounds, words that change inside, gender, cases, plurals and agreement. Easier: no tones — pitch does not change a word —, no measure words (numbers stand right before the noun), no separable verb–object words like 吃饭, and no serial verbs. Arabic has one “we” (نَحْنُ) for both 我们 and 咱们, distinguishes voiced and voiceless (د d / ت t) rather than aspirated and plain, and has no retroflex sounds and no ü: ص and ط are emphatic, not zh / ch.

New: letters joined right to left, words that change inside, gender, cases, plurals and agreement. Familiar: the adjective after the noun (nhà lớn ≈ بَيْتٌ كَبِيرٌ), the owner after the thing (sách của tôi ≈ كِتَابِي) and no “is” before an adjective. Arabic has no tones, no classifiers, no implosive ɓ / ɗ, no aspirated th set against t, no serial verbs, no polite particles, no capital letters, and one “we” (نَحْنُ) for both chúng ta and chúng tôi.

Familiar: the dual (two of anything has its own form), possessive endings on nouns, person endings that make pronouns unnecessary, and the uvular q (Arabic ق). New: short separate words instead of one long word — no noun incorporation, no antipassive, no applicatives —, prepositions, gender, subjects marked the same way with every verb (no ergative), no evidential endings such as -guuq (“reportedly”), sentences joined with conjunctions instead of verb moods, and a script read right to left.
